subChunks.title: Component Extraction and Reuse
subChunks.hookHtml: At some point, you'll have a button with fifteen utility classes repeated in six files. When the designer changes the border radius, you'll update it in all six places. This lesson covers the three strategies for managing repetition in a Tailwind codebase — and crucially, which one is right in which situation.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The three strategies

  1. React/framework components — extract a <Button> component. The classes live in JSX. Correct in 95% of cases.
  2. @utility / @apply — create a CSS class that bundles utilities. Use only for HTML you don't control (markdown output, third-party widgets).
  3. Multi-cursor editing — if 2–3 identical elements are in one file. Not scalable.

Strategy 1 — React components (the right approach)

/* BEFORE: classes repeated across many files */
<button className="inline-flex items-center px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700
                   text-white text-sm font-medium rounded-md transition-colors
                   disabled:opacity-50 disabled:cursor-not-allowed">

/* AFTER: extract a Button component */
function Button({ children, variant = 'primary', ...props }) {
  const base = 'inline-flex items-center px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium rounded-md transition-colors disabled:opacity-50 disabled:cursor-not-allowed';
  const variants = {
    primary:   'bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white',
    secondary: 'bg-white hover:bg-gray-50 text-gray-900 border border-gray-300',
    ghost:     'bg-transparent hover:bg-gray-100 text-gray-700',
  };
  return <button className={`${base} ${variants[variant]}`} {...props}>{children}</button>;
}

Strategy 2 — @utility (the v4 way)

/* index.css — define a custom utility class */
@utility btn-primary {
  @apply inline-flex items-center px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700
         text-white text-sm font-medium rounded-md transition-colors;
}

/* The @layer components approach from v3 also still works */
@layer components {
  .btn-legacy {
    @apply inline-flex items-center px-4 py-2 bg-gray-600 text-white rounded-md;
  }
}

Use @apply when styling HTML you don't write: markdown renderer output, third-party widgets, global base styles for HTML elements.

Do not use @apply for React components — use a component instead.

The extraction rule — don't extract prematurely

/* If you have this in ONE file — don't extract */
{items.map(item => (
  <div key={item.id} className="bg-white p-4 rounded-lg shadow-sm">
    {item.name}
  </div>
))}
/* This is already DRY — the className appears once, rendered many times */

Wait until you have the same styles in 3+ distinct places before extracting. Premature abstraction makes refactoring harder.

cn() — conditional class composition

import { clsx } from 'clsx';
import { twMerge } from 'tailwind-merge';

function cn(...inputs) {
  return twMerge(clsx(inputs));
}

/* Usage */
function Button({ className, variant = 'primary', ...props }) {
  return (
    <button
      className={cn(
        'inline-flex items-center px-4 py-2 rounded-md font-medium text-sm transition-colors',
        variant === 'primary' && 'bg-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-700 text-white',
        variant === 'secondary' && 'bg-white border border-gray-300 hover:bg-gray-50',
        className  // caller can extend/override
      )}
      {...props}
    />
  );
}

twMerge removes conflicting Tailwind classes — if a caller passes className="bg-red-600", it removes bg-blue-600 from the base instead of stacking both.

Maester Cordell: "When the same utility string appears in three places, you have a decision. In a React project, the answer is almost always: make a component. The classes stay in JSX where Tailwind can find them. The abstraction lives where abstractions belong — in the language."

storyBeats.speaker: Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: When the same utility string appears in three places, you have a decision. In a React project, the answer is almost always the same: make a component. The classes stay in JSX where Tailwind can find them. The abstraction lives where abstractions belong — in the language.

storyBeats.speaker: Button component (the right approach)
Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: @apply has its place — when you're styling HTML you didn't write. A markdown renderer's output. A third-party widget. Not your own React components. Use @apply there and you've rebuilt BEM on top of Tailwind. That is not a trade worth making.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a button system showing three variants using the correct class pattern:

  • All .btn-base elements share: inline-flex, items-center, px-4, py-2, rounded-md, font-medium, text-sm, transition-colors, duration-150
  • .btn-primary adds: bg-blue-600, hover:bg-blue-700, text-white
  • .btn-secondary adds: bg-white, hover:bg-gray-50, text-gray-900, border, border-gray-300
  • .btn-ghost adds: bg-transparent, hover:bg-gray-100, text-gray-700
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build an alert/notification component system with three variants — success (green), warning (amber), error (red) — from scratch. Each variant needs an icon area, a title, and a description. Use consistent spacing and a colour-coded left border accent. No starter HTML provided.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the three approaches to managing repeated utility classes in a Tailwind codebase. When is each one appropriate? Why does the Tailwind team recommend components over @apply for React projects? What does tailwind-merge add that clsx alone cannot do?

questions.prompt: What does tailwind-merge solve that plain clsx does not?
options: Removes conflicting Tailwind classes (e.g. two bg- classes) — keeping only the last one
Adds TypeScript types to className strings
Generates class names at build time
questions.answer: Removes conflicting Tailwind classes (e.g. two bg- classes) — keeping only the last one
questions.explanation: clsx only handles conditional inclusion of class strings — it doesn't know anything about Tailwind. If you end up with both bg-blue-600 and bg-red-600, clsx passes both through and CSS specificity determines which wins (unpredictably). tailwind-merge understands Tailwind's class groups and removes the conflicting class, keeping only the last one.

questions.prompt: You're building a React app and your card component appears in 20 places with identical styling. What is the correct approach?
options: Extract a Card React component with the classes in JSX
Create a .card class with @apply in your CSS file
Use CSS variables to parameterise the classes
Repeat the classes each time — that is the Tailwind way
questions.answer: Extract a Card React component with the classes in JSX
questions.explanation: In a component-based framework, the component IS the abstraction. Extract a Card component and keep the Tailwind classes in JSX. This keeps Tailwind's scanning working correctly, co-locates styles with markup, and provides a single source of truth to update.

questions.prompt: A team heavily uses @apply for all their components over six months: .card, .btn, .badge with modifier classes like .btn-sm, .btn-danger. They now have 40+ component classes. What problem have they created?
options: They've rebuilt BEM on top of Tailwind — losing all composition advantages. They now maintain both a utility system and a component class system. Fix: use React components with variant props instead
They've hit Tailwind's 50-class limit — @apply doesn't support more than 50 uses per project
The @apply classes will conflict with Tailwind's generated utilities in production builds
No problem — @apply is the official recommended pattern for all components
questions.answer: They've rebuilt BEM on top of Tailwind — losing all composition advantages. They now maintain both a utility system and a component class system. Fix: use React components with variant props instead
questions.explanation: This is the most common Tailwind anti-pattern in team codebases. The @apply approach feels familiar to CSS developers, but it reintroduces all the problems Tailwind was designed to solve: styles in separate files from markup, unclear class relationships, specificity conflicts, and growing CSS file size. Component + variants map (or CVA) is the scalable solution.
